title: Toyota Production System from supermarket pull experiments to plant and supplier diffusion
pressure: Postwar Japanese automobile producers faced low volumes, capital scarcity, diverse models and demand uncertainty, making U.S.-style long runs and large inventories economically difficult. Toyota needed high variety with low inventory and rapid problem response.
preExistingWorldModel: Flow production, Ford-style moving lines and Toyota’s earlier jidoka ideas existed. The open question was how to synchronize processes and suppliers under smaller, variable demand without creating either shortages or excessive inventory.
candidateRoutes: copy high-volume push production with large batches
local inventory buffers at each process
jidoka/line stop and rapid abnormality response
observationsAndInstruments: Taiichi Ohno studied supermarket replenishment logic and adapted downstream consumption/pull ideas to factory material flow.
Toyota experimented with kanban in machine shops, then expanded it across plants; official Toyota history places whole-company deployment through the early 1960s.
Jidoka/andon and standardized work made abnormalities visible and allowed production to stop/correct rather than hide defects in inventory.
Toyota extended kanban practices to major suppliers through the 1960s, showing that plant-local pull depended on external coordination.
The system evolved through repeated shop-floor experiments rather than appearing as one finished “lean” blueprint.
decisiveTests: Pull signaling had to reduce work-in-process without creating chronic line starvation.
Shorter setup/lot practices had to make mixed-model production feasible at lower volumes.
Supplier adoption had to preserve delivery/replenishment reliability across organizational boundaries.
Quality/problem-response practices had to prevent low inventory from simply exposing failures without a correction mechanism.
technicalOrScientificTransition: Toyota developed a coupled production-control system in which material flow, information signals, quality response, standardized work and supplier coordination co-evolved. The method was conditioned by a specific demand/capital environment rather than derived from one universal factory optimum.
rivalsAndFailures: Kanban alone is not the whole Toyota Production System and can fail if process reliability or replenishment discipline is absent.
Low inventory is an outcome/control strategy, not evidence that every buffer is waste under every stochastic regime.
Later “lean” labels can compress decades of Toyota-specific experiments and supplier institutions into a portable recipe.
diffusionAndScaling: Toyota extended kanban from internal shops to all plants and then suppliers by the mid/late 1960s; broader international diffusion of “lean” language occurred later.
standardsAndInstitutions: Toyota plants, supplier associations, production-control functions and shop-floor teams held different operating knowledge; routines and tacit training were as important as written kanban rules.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Tighter coupled supply can shift inventory/risk to suppliers and become fragile under disruptions; these system boundaries become especially visible in later epochs.
secondOrderEffects: The production system changed the future improvement loop itself by making problems visible, shortening feedback and embedding iterative process improvement into routine operations.
sourceNativeSummary: Toyota’s HD5 trajectory is not “invent kanban.” Supermarket pull was one experiment inside a larger coupled system of flow, visual problem detection, standardized work, supplier coordination and repeated shop-floor learning.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: Which TPS practices were independently present elsewhere but later retrospectively grouped under Toyota/lean?
How much performance depended on Japan/Toyota-specific labor and supplier institutions that limited portability?
